A1.justification: Both PDFs describe OpenVLThinker's iterative SFT-RL approach. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A-C are readable and support comparison despite substantial revision.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark evaluations, filtering experiments, GRPO training analyses, and a 100-example ConTextual study in Appendix A.

after.justification: v2 reports original six-benchmark evaluations, a 3B-model experiment, curriculum and reasoning analyses, and the retained ConTextual study.

M1.justification: v1 progressively adjusts training sources across iterations. v2 introduces a substantive two-stage curriculum within each iteration: combine GPT-4o difficulty ratings with base-model errors, normalize and cluster sources, then train sequentially on medium and hard data. The underlying iterative SFT-GRPO loop remains.

E1.justification: v2 adds MMMU-Pro, EMMA, and HallusionBench, extending evaluation beyond visual mathematics to multidisciplinary reasoning and hallucination/perception. Its training pool adds ChartQA, DVQA, A-OKVQA, UniGeo, and GeoQA while dropping AI2D and ScienceQA. ConTextual remains in Appendix A, and MathVision-mini remains in analyses.

E2.justification: The main comparison expands substantially beyond Qwen2.5-VL-7B and GPT-4o, adding Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Mulberry, InternVL2.5, Kimi-VL, Qwen2-VL, R1-VL, and VLAA-Thinker rows. R1-Onevision, already evaluated in v1 Table 4, joins the broader comparison in v2 Table 1. v2 also introduces a separate small-model comparison in Table 2.

E3.justification: v1 uses 25K initial SFT examples, 5K in later SFT rounds, and 5K per RL round; v2 reports 3K SFT plus 3K medium and 6K hard RL examples per cycle. Initial captioning changes from Qwen2.5-VL-3B to 7B, and the reasoning teacher changes from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B to QwQ-32B. A single-cycle 3B experiment and fixed-3K difficulty controls are added. Appendix B's optimizer and inference settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds reasoning-keyword analysis, a direct-RL-without-SFT observation, medium-versus-mixed-difficulty controls, curriculum-versus-hard-only comparisons, and reasoning-length distributions across iterations and incorrect answers. Appendix C replaces early GRPO examples with paired SFT-incorrect/RL-correct cases. v1's training curves and initial teacher length/pass@4 analyses are removed; Appendix A's captioning and refinement analyses remain.

E5.justification: Neither version reports training-seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The additional descriptive plots and point accuracies in v2 do not introduce uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces the trained model's MathVista/MathVerse/MathVision scores of 70.2/47.9/25.3 with 72.3/50.3/25.9 under the revised training configuration. v2 adds general-reasoning and perception results and a 63.4 MathVista result for OpenVLThinker-3B. Table 3's filtering results also change. The final MathVision-mini row disappears from the main table, although mini-set analyses remain. Appendix A's results are unchanged.

T1.justification: Section 4.3 introduces a composite source-difficulty score defined as the average of independently z-normalized GPT-4o ratings and base-model error rates. This is a limited mathematical definition supporting the curriculum. Section 3's probabilistic formulation, SFT loss, and GRPO objective remain unchanged, with no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: v2 expands the central claims from preliminary visual-math improvement to six-benchmark effectiveness, reduced hallucination, and competitiveness with contemporary reasoners using substantially less training data. It also elevates the role of SFT in highlighting latent reasoning actions into an explicit contribution in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 develops v1's SFT warm-start hypothesis into a specific account of keyword-triggered reasoning actions and constrained RL exploration. It adds interpretations of difficulty-matched curricula and increasingly concise reasoning. New limitations address untested real-world robustness and larger backbones, although the statement that only 7B was validated conflicts with the new 3B experiment.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies full fine-tuning, H100-80GB-class computing resources, approximately 30 minutes for SFT and 20 hours for RL per iteration, and eight hours for verified data generation. Hyperparameter tables, the caption prompt, and resource links remain. Conversely, v1's explicit four-candidate distillation setting and binary correctness-only/no-format-reward specification are no longer supplied for the revised training; this does not establish an actual reward change.

R1.justification: Section 2.2 substantially expands and differentiates distillation, direct-RL, and recent visual-reasoning approaches, adding discussion of works such as Visual-RFT, VL-Rethinker, NoisyRollout, and R1-VL. The paper positions its contribution more specifically around SFT's role and data-efficient iteration relative to concurrent reasoners, rather than primarily aligning with early explorations.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. v2 reorganizes the chronological training narrative into method subsections and a separate Experiments section, adds explicit contribution bullets and limitations, and relocates the filtering discussion. Much of Appendices A and B is retained.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the opening benchmark chart and training pipeline, restructures Table 1 around model rows and grouped benchmark columns, and adds keyword, difficulty, curriculum, and iteration-distribution displays. Several earlier plots and example panels are replaced. The ConTextual plot is retained and relocated from v1 Figure 7 to v2 Figure 11.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation of generalization and training choices through broader benchmarks, contemporary comparator coverage, fixed-size difficulty controls, and curriculum ablations. These additions provide stronger evidence for the approach beyond higher headline scores. Reporting defects temper the improvement: Sections 5.1 and 6 give a 46.6 average despite Table 1's 47.9, and Section 5.1's 2.7-point HallusionBench gain conflicts with the table's 1.6 points. Some reward details are also lost. Nevertheless, the strengthened empirical support constitutes a substantial net improvement.
